page: Google Cloud Platform c4n-highcpu-16 is an x86_64 instance type belonging to the Network Optimized machine family. The system provision provides 16 dedicated vCPUs coupled with 32 GB of system memory, yielding a 1:2 compute-to-memory ratio of 2.0 GB of RAM per vCPU. It does not include integrated GPU accelerators and offers no local ephemeral storage, requiring reliance on external block storage devices for operating system and data retention needs.

Hardware resource distribution prioritizes raw processing density over memory overhead. With 16 dedicated execution threads and no complimentary public IPv4 addresses included by default, networking infrastructure must be managed through cloud network routing or assigned external IP resources. The lean memory profile minimizes unutilized memory capacity for applications that are primarily compute-bound and network-centric.

From a cost-efficiency perspective, the high-CPU footprint avoids the expense of surplus memory when hosting compute-dominated processes. The configuration is suitable for network appliances, reverse proxies, ingress load balancers, API gateways, traffic routing layers, and horizontally scaled microservices that require dedicated CPU execution without high memory footprints.
description: Google Cloud Platform c4n-highcpu-16 is a network-optimized compute instance designed for network-intensive and processing-heavy applications. Built on the x86_64 architecture, the server features 16 dedicated vCPUs paired with 32 GB of memory, establishing a 2.0 GB per core ratio aligned with compute-focused profiles. It does not include discrete GPU accelerators and comes with no bundled local storage, directing all storage requirements to attached network volumes. Furthermore, no complimentary public IPv4 addresses are assigned at provisioning. The compact memory allocation relative to core count maintains resource efficiency by reducing idle memory overhead during compute-intensive tasks. Consequently, the c4n-highcpu-16 is suited for network appliances, high-traffic proxy servers, load balancing layers, web serving, and distributed microservice workloads.
